Not indictments

These are not sealed indictments and the guys keeping the chart up to date have now admitted that fact.

They have agreed that the criticism of the work was correct and they have changed the language they use. They have had to make this change because the truth is many things are sealed within PACER not just indictments. However, they have not fully addressed the shortcomings of their methodology because among other things there's simply no way to tell how many sealed indictments exist using their numbers.

As recently as November 2018 they were still using Sealed Indictments in their chart https://pbs.twimg.com/media/DtdXEVRUwAAk7Lk.jpg

Sealed Court Proceedings

So what do their numbers show? They now say "Sealed Cases" in their title and the even more accurate "new sealed court proceedings" in their footnotes. Also, notice in their footnote, they mention that in some of these cases have become unsealed (they don't say how many) and some smaller number removed. That fact that sealed court proceedings can become unsealed was one of the primaries criticism of why their numbers were useless.* Many proceedings that are sealed become unsealed in a short period of time. The sealed indictment for the NXVIM guy was sealed for just 24 hours.

To illustrate why counting just new number is inaccurate, using a rough example, you could get 5,000 new sealed proceedings a week come in, but you could also have a total that never went above 15,000 if many of the cases were unsealed very quickly. If the flow is fast enough, you don't build up a backlog. It's like a factory can build a million screws a month, but only have 50,000 screws in inventory if they ship them out the door fast enough.

There's no baseline for comparison

*Their numbers are still problematic and we don't know if this is an unusual number or not.

The one report where these items were tracked and counted was done in 2008 for cases from the year 2006. So the baseline they compared to was not sealed court proceedings per month or per year, but sealed court proceedings that remained sealed around two years later. They chose 2006 precisely because they didn't want to count cases tha became unsealed quickly.

Method

We decided to examine all cases filed in 2006. A calendar-year filing cohort is suitable for this study, because courts incorporate the filing year into case numbers, and a complete calendar-year filing cohort affords accounting for complete sequences of case numbers. The more recent the cases we look at, the more likely information about them will be available electronically; because we began the study early in 2008, selecting cases filed in 2006 avoided cases sealed only for very short periods of time soon after their filing.

You can find the report here and just looking through the table of contents, you can see how many different types of proceedings are sealed.
